I don't wish to go over all of that again but let me first ask you does that video fairly and accurately reflect the terrain as you knew it in the southern end of Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although it seems that the sky was overcast when the picture was taken, we can see the factory in Zeleni Jadar, we can see the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road and the facilities of Rajine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can I focus your attention on the screen at the hair-pin turn, you see there a road that winds down to the valley floor in a series of curves. And then the last turn is a 180-degree turn into the valley. Can you confirm that this -- and I can tell you that north is as marked on the video so you can see the north-south axis there. Can you confirm that that last curve is the southern limit of the urban area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first and the last time that I entered Srebrenica from that direction. I was surprised to see how steep the approaches are, how curvy the road is, and this specific curve which is almost 360 degrees marks the age of the urban and developed part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's continue now rolling the tape through 4 minutes and 5 seconds. And just for the record, again, this is 4D682.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Actually let's just stop it here for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I realise that you only spent a very short time in Srebrenica town, but does the layout of the town, the road layout correspond to your recollection of what that was like in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember clearly the main street, the department store, and the Hotel Domavija. I have seen those buildings, I passed by them, I also know where the police station is because I spent a night there. I wasn't very much impressed by the rest of the buildings and therefore I cannot remember them. And I also remember the post office, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue rolling the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, first of all, General, I'd just like to go back to the commander's reconnaissance and you've told us a little bit about the commander's reconnaissance and your observations and your ability to observe. And what I'd like to know is whether you learned that there were Bosnian army positions in Srebrenica town during the commander's reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the command of the 28th Division was in Srebrenica. We had information that they were using the post office as their communications centre and that they were also using the Domavija Hotel. Also a hunter's lodge was being mentioned, but I don't know exactly where that building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And did you learn more as your forces approached Srebrenica town? And we've now seen from the video, graphically, how that would have looked and the extent to which those forces would have had a view on the town and vice versa. Did you come to learn from reports or based on your personal observations about whether there were any facilities being used for military purposes in the town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the Hotel Domavija, the post office and the hunter's lodge were used for military purposes. Whether there were any other facilities used for these same purposes, I didn't know at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports of firing emanating from anywhere in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were exposed to mortar fire directly from the town; however, at the time I didn't know their exact positions because it was impossible to spot them from the posts or the positions where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 4D210, please, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This one is still in your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This should be page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S version, and we're looking for items D, E, and F.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is did you hear that the commands of the 282nd, 283rd, and 284th Brigades were located in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document that we are talking about now relates to mobilisation and reorganisation of the 28th Division; and here, elements of the 282 and 283 brigades are mentioned and they have their bases in Srebrenica. In other words, that means that elements of these brigades were deployed in the town itself, probably at command posts or the logistic units and communications centre whereas the battalions and companies were deployed close to the UNPROFOR checkpoints on the Zeleni-Jadar-Srebrenica axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 4D135 again, please. This is page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S. And I'd like to focus on section 1, item 1. It states that: "The command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica" -- well, let me back up and explain what this document is again. This is again the defence ministry document, and the subject line is: "List of office space used by the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Item 1, 1, refers to the command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica located at a place called Lovac feature, Stari Grad, Srebrenica. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I understood that to be a hunter's lodge but since they say Lovac here, I suppose it's the same building where the command of the 8th OG was, whereas in July 1995 that was actually the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we have 4D671, please. For those of you who have the benefit of the trial books that we have just distributed, this is image number 18, and the title of it is: "Google Earth image Srebrenica town zoomed on the southern end."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Looking at this image, can you locate on this image the location of the hunting lodge that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where this building called Lovac is. In addition to that, all I can say is that it was in town. I'd rather not guess by looking at this image; however, it might be or it must be within the reach of main roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have the assistance of the usher, please, I would like to have an image placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, does that refresh your recollection as to where the hunting lodge was located? Was it located where the circle is drawn?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it's becoming obvious, I think, that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I should ask you now that you've seen the marking, does that remind you that that's where it was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We can remove that from the ELMO. Could we have 4D8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is an unsigned report by the State Security Service of the Bosnian Ministry of the Interior, it's dated the 28th of August, 1995, and in effect, this appears to be a post mortem on the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it looks like to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There is a heading which says: "Continued description of negotiations," and then below that, it says: "The division command was in the old town sector and the hunting lodge. On the last day, 11 July 1995, it was impossible to approach this building because it was under constant fire from the Chetniks." Now, sir, my question is do you have any -- now that you've seen this, do you have any independent recollection about whether you received reports of combat going on around this facility?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any specific report indicating that units fired at this facility, at least my units didn't. Whether those were units from the Bratunac Brigade or the support units for the corps, that is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Can we have 4D135 now again. I'd like to go to page 2 of the English; and on the B/C/S, it's just at the very bottom of page 1, going over to page 2. It's item 4, number 1. Referring to the 282nd Brigade, it says -- this again is the listing of office space used by various units, and it says: "Domavija Hotel, Srebrenica, used by the 282nd Brigade, the area covers 427 square metres; purpose, office space of the brigade command depot, kitchen and training hall." Now, perhaps we could just put 4D670 back up on the screen, please, if it's not still there. This should be image 17 in your books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, by any chance can you make out the location of the Hotel Domavija on this image?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that Hotel Domavija from this sharp curve that we already mentioned is more to the east or somewhat to the south as well. It's just beneath the slopes where some mineral springs are. However, in this map, it could be here in the upper right-hand corner or even -- well, I'm not quite sure. I was near the hotel in Srebrenica when we entered, but I really can't find my bearings with this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In any event, sir, the hotel is on this image; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you are showing it to me, it's possible and I'm sure that it is. However, at that time, I didn't have a bird's view of the city or the town so that I know exactly which building is. If I were to go to Srebrenica, I would be able to locate Hotel Domavija immediately. It is possible that it's within this complex just below the forest area, because I remember the forest quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that's very helpful, and I'm grateful for your patience because I understand that you did not have a bird's eye view in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to 4D135 for one last location. This will be English page 2 and B/C/S page 2. And it's item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Referring to the 284th Brigade, it says: "Directorate of the Radnik GP Construction Company Srebrenica. Total area of the 284th Brigade is 187 square metres. The feature is used for the command of the 284th." Does the Radnik -- does that name Radnik GP Construction Company mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now where this building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to put it to you that that is the same location as the shopping centre, would that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know where the department store used to be and where it probably still is. It's in downtown on the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're done with the video and the images for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony, you were asked about a mobilisation order --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that was 1D698. If we could have that put up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As I understand it, this is the mobilisation order for -- from the Drina Corps command, dated the 15th of July. This is a mobilisation of non-assigned conscripts and it's a request -- I'm sorry. It's not an order, it's a request.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to -- sir, if you could just take that request out of your binder, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And on e-court I would like to have 4D650, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: 1D698 is a request in respect of the Zvornik area --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is clearly an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I was just reading from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you get to the end and General Krstic tells somebody to do something, I think it's pretty clear what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. I think you've both made things clear and I think we know what we're talking about here. Go straight to your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you wish to refer to any particular part of this document, please do so straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at 4D650, whether it be characterised as an order or a request, 4D650 is a request or order in respect of various other municipalities, namely, Vlasenica, Milici, Skelani, Bratunac, and Sekovici. Are these two, when you compare these documents, are they in the same form?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both documents have the same purpose, they were signed - if I can read it - Assistant Chief of Staff for organisation and mobilisation of the Drina Corps command, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic. And in the heading, he properly said "request." The document which refers to the conscripts in the area of Zvornik is fully in compliance with the legal processes. And the other one that we see on the screen now contains some terms that can be interpreted as orders, and this is not the way to address draft offices. However, since this document was also forwarded to the brigades, Mr. Jovicic decided to use these terms that are stronger and then can sound as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you prefer to have the break now, Mr. McCloskey or do you wish to start straight away?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can get started and I can probably just deal with the some of the Borovcanin issues since we can remember those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's start. Your estimate is still of around 20 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll have a better idea at the end of the day. I hope it's less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope very much that it's less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to say something before Mr. McCloskey takes to the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before all the Defence teams started their cross-examinations, I had a list of exhibits that are going to be used and therefore I would be obliged if Mr. McCloskey could provide me with a similar list because I would like to know in advance what lies ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I suppose you have made that list available to Mr. Haynes already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- but that doesn't necessarily mean that the witness has a copy of it. We have a copy of it. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you'll know it came through a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And General Pandurevic is quite correct, we were having some debate as to what the current state of practice was because your original order, in fact, states that lists should be served the minute the witness takes the witness stand, but it's sort of fallen into abeyance. Everybody else provided me with advanced copies, by which I mean days in advance of their cross-examination. The Prosecution list has just come through. Perhaps we can take the break and he can see the list now; and if it is such as he would like to consider it longer before the cross-examination starts, I'll let you know after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think it runs to 20-odd pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The rule, as we have always understood it, was that the list is sent out at the start of cross-examination. So I don't know where this is coming from. That's the rule we're going on. If the General wants to see the battle plan before the battle, no objection. I think that's consistent with your previous ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, as you would expect us to do, we have got together to see how best we can proceed without any risk of losing any court time. However, I feel I must say something historical about all this because I was rather surprised to hear Mr. McCloskey say in answer to Mr. Pandurevic's request that he didn't know where this coming from. And for his benefit, where it was coming from was the Trial Chamber's order of the 26th of May, chapter 3 of which reads: "Lists of documents or other material to be used by the Prosecution and the other Defence teams when cross-examining a Defence witness must be disclosed to the Defence calling the witness at the commencement of the examination-in-chief of that witness after the witness has made the solemn declaration pursuant to Rule 90(a) of the rules. "H: Concurrently the Prosecution and the other Defence teams must release to the Defence team calling the witness via the e-court system any documents or other material not already in the possession of the Defence team calling the witness that form part of the lists of the documents or material to be used during cross-examination." I pause there. There are therefore two obligations, mandatory obligations. One, to serve a list; the other to disclose. They are separate and divisible in my view. "I: Should the Prosecution or the other Defence teams seek to use a document or material during cross-examination that has not been listed and disclosed, they may be permitted to do so on sharing good cause for not listing it and disclosing it." I pause again. On the face of it, the however many, 400-and-odd documents on this list would need to have your leave to be used at this point in time. "J: In such a case and if the need arises, the Defence team calling the witness may then request a short adjournment of the proceedings to examine the said document or material." Now, it's none of my business here to cause anybody embarrassment but I have raised the contents of this order with everybody here prior to my client going into the witness box and the response from the Defence teams has been voluntarily to disclose their list of documents well in advance. The practice heretofore, frankly, I don't care about. My client is the only accused who has gone into the witness box, and as an accused, as per your more recent order, he stands in a very different position to any other witness in the case. He's entitled to know, in my submission, all the material upon which the Prosecution rely and that includes all material which they might use in his cross-examination. The list which has just been served, I haven't counted them, runs to 23 pages and I'm guessing something approaching 500 documents. 183 of them are entirely new to this case. They've never appeared on a 65 ter list or any list of exhibits before, and in my submission, Mr. Pandurevic is entitled to see those documents and all the documents that might be used in the case against him. However, as I said, I have no wish to cause a hiatus in proceedings and I've spoken to Mr. McCloskey and the mode of procedure, I think we can agree upon, is that he can get started with his cross-examination, he can deal with what he terms the Borovcanin issues, and we will suck it and see thereafter; but I've made it plain I would prefer it if during the course of the remainder of today, no new document were used in cross-examination. And on that basis, I think we can probably fill the day's proceedings without my needing to ask you simply to adjourn so that General Pandurevic can see all of these new documents that have been placed upon this list at this moment in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Do you agree, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In part. I don't necessarily read the Court's order exactly how he reads it. I'd have to go back and look at it again. We never received any lists from any Defence for any cross until it was started, according to what I am told. And we have assembled this list, it's been an ongoing thing. We finished it, well, last night and a few more this morning. If they need more time to prepare, I have no objection to that. But I would like to get started and I don't think there is going to be any big surprises here. There's not meant to be any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start and then play it by ear. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to raise a quick issue concerning the 183 documents which are new to this case and which have been added to this list. A preliminary review of those documents reveals that there are documents to which we will object being used during cross-examination of this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There are many documents from the 1993 period which I really had no intention of going into; however, they spent days in 1993 as -- on issues of opening the column and there is a lot of documents on those issues and I have brought those documents and other documents in that I did not originally intend to to respond to issues. So I don't know what the 189 really is at this point, but they are in response to issues that have been raised by and large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If my colleagues agree we'll deal with that as and if it arises. So let's start with your cross-examination and your claimed rights, Mr. Haynes, for the time are put on hold but reserved, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't, of course, need to introduce each other. We have spoken many years ago now, as counsel brought out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me start by, just because it's fresh in my mind, some of the Borovcanin issues that were brought up and are related actually to your other testimony in some ways. You may recall that Miroslav Deronjic has testified and that his testimony from a previous hearing is part of the evidence in this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when Deronjic said that he went to see President Karadzic on the 8th or 9th of July and he was -- said something about requesting Karadzic to bring in Mr. Borovcanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but I can't remember any specific details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely the few thoughts that you've shared with us, the thoughts contained in the couple of sentences that you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Basically that -- and I haven't looked at the testimony either, I'm going on my recollection, that one of the reasons he went to see him was to suggest he bring in Ljubisa Borovcanin and his unit because they were a good unit and that they could assist in the Srebrenica case -- the Srebrenica battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer the question. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to questions being asked about evidence in this case. What's the point of having the witness offer characterisations about statements that are in evidence under 92 quater? It's a pointless exercise. It's not what the Chamber should be hearing. It's not evidence. The statement itself is evidence and his commentary or his recollection of what that statement might say really serves no purpose for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've been bringing up facts from other witnesses and evidence to help form the foundation of a question for two and a half, three years. I don't think there's anything prejudicial or problematic about that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the understanding that we don't know whether this is a solitary question or whether it's to be followed by others on the same, for the time being, we believe that it is a perfectly legitimate question and you may proceed with your answer, Mr. Pandurevic. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we at least have a page reference, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's coming, I suppose. Yes, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think I'm required to give a page reference to something that I remember during an hour of cross-examination, and in this situation, if that was a requirement, it would have us to stop and go -- so far the General and I agree on what was roughly said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. And if it becomes more complicated then we will ask you for a reference for sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because the -- I've got some excellent folks here, e-court page is 242, 284 to 290, and the testimony is P3139.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in your history from being a commander in Bosnia from I think it was April of 1992 through the end of the war, were you ever in a position where SDS officials brought in units of their choosing to assist you in your operations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such situation. I don't remember any member of the SDS being involved in any such thing. However, I'm familiar with a similar situation, situations of a similar nature. Certain municipal authorities would set their own priorities of the war and they would try to exert influence on the president of the republic and the Main Staff in order to have some priority actions being carried out in the territory of their municipality rather than elsewhere. I suppose that some or most of these municipal leaders belonged to the SDS. However, their requests were not of political or partisan nature. I believe that such requests were justified by some other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But we can agree in this situation that the Borovcanin unit coming to assist in Srebrenica was something that was helpful.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the operation was launched, I didn't know that the MUP would participate in any way. I knew that there was a special MUP brigade. I don't know whether Mr. Deronjic specifically requested for that brigade because it was special and because it was a good combat unit. I suppose that that must have been the reason and I wouldn't say that it was because Mr. Borovcanin was the deputy commander of the brigade. I don't know what reasons governed Deronjic, however, my post festum information says that the keys of Srebrenica had already been obtained before the unit under the command of Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin was introduced into fighting and engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The keys to Srebrenica, yes, the keys to Potocari, no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In combat terms, Potocari had its door ajar, if we are going to use figurative speech, and Borovcanin had to do some security tasks in terms of controlling the remaining forces scouring of the terrain because some forces had opted for that direction to pull out of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where on the morning of the 12th of July, a Bratunac Brigade soldier was killed by a mine clearing a minefield for Mr. Borovcanin and his units; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, he was opening a passage through the minefield that had been set by the Bratunac Brigade. On the 12th, we were not aware of all the intentions of the 28th Division. It was only logical because of that for Mr. Borovcanin and his units to be engaged on the direction between Bratunac and Potocari and I mean primarily the village of Milacevici, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you agree with me a Bratunac Brigade soldier was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I return to my original objection, because I believe that what we're now hearing is evidence about evidence. Now I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we have been doing that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But Mr. President, there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may, there is a distinction between using evidence in order to provoke a memory of firsthand knowledge of observations of things that really happened. If this is going to turn into a long cross-examination series of questions and answers about this case, well, then I would suggest that that's improper, but of course, it's not improper to ask a question to provoke a memory of what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as you know, Lieutenant-Colonel, at the time, Pandurevic was in the area that we're talking about. He said he went through Potocari on the night of the 11th. These are all interrelated to this case. This is an absurd objection and it should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You don't need to use such dramatic and harsh language, Mr. McCloskey. Let us decide. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps a way out of this is simply if Mr. McCloskey inquires when the General came by the information as to the death of the Bratunac Brigade that may, as it were, help you decide what weight this evidence has got, whether it's direct evidence or a commentary on what he's read in the course of the last few years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, when the General suggests to me that the fighting is over and that Borovcanin maybe just had a little security work, I think it's perfectly fair for me to remind him of a soldier's death, that this was still going on, that this was more than security work. This is cross-examination. That's what this is -- this is what's going on here. That's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are unanimous on this. For the time being you may proceed, Mr. McCloskey, and I think you were about to put another question, the previous one had been answered. Correct me if I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I really don't recall, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just trying to get him to confirm that an answer to my first question that there was a Bratunac soldier that was killed helping Borovcanin's unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will agree with you that I only heard about that during this trial. Srebrenica fell on the 11th but the fighting against the 28th Division was not completed and it is in that sense that Mr. Borovcanin was given certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you may recall in the discussion that Deronjic said that the president made comments about the solution of Western Slavonia. Do you know what President Karadzic was talking about when he talked about Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this statement by Mr. Deronjic a long time ago. I did not listen to his testimony so it's very hard for me to speak of all the details and we all know only too well what happened in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's something that from Mr. Deronjic's testimony was very important for him and very important for the president, but could you tell us your perspective, just briefly. I don't want a long story of Western Slavonia, but what was he talking about? What was the Serb perception of what happened to Serbs in Western Slavonia not long before this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army won a major victory in Western Slavonia, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there allegations of abuse of civilians by the Croatians against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Serbian population left the area, they fled the area, and as far as I know, there were no charges brought for that. Nothing has happened so far to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't President Karadzic think that as those civilians were leaving that they were victimised and shot and killed, some of them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Karadzic meant, but we know what the situation was in Potocari. The Muslim civilian population did not scatter and run through the forest. They were not shot at in the forest. Instead they all gathered in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The question calls for speculation. It asks -- the question is what does -- what did President Karadzic think? How is this witness going to tell us what President Karadzic may have thought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's based on the statement that Mr. Deronjic said and it's based on what Mr. Karadzic said to Deronjic that Serbs were victimised as they were forced to leave Western Slavonia and as he told this to Deronjic he was very upset and was suggesting the same thing happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's in evidence and I want to find out if any of that from the President got its way down to the troops on the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected by my colleagues but I read your question when you used word "think" is was it as meaning the -- was it the belief of President Karadzic that those civilians were victimised, shot and killed. So as far as I am concerned, unless I -- yes, okay, then please, Mr. Pandurevic, go ahead and answer the question, please. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, he has already answered you in a way so do you want to pursue the matter further --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or do you want to move to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On July 11th, were you aware of what had happened to the Serbs in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Western Slavonia happened in May of that year but on the 11th of July, I was not thinking of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But were you aware that it had happened, that Serbs had been victimised in Western Slavonia by Croats?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew. Maybe the president had in mind that whole situation and didn't want something like that to happen to the Muslims; he wanted us to act differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps. Perhaps. Now, when General Mladic, on the 11th of July, looked into the camera and said something like, Now on the anniversary of the uprising against the Dahijes, it's time to take revenge upon the Turks in this area," what do you think he meant by that? And I think we've established what the uprising against the Dahis is, so I don't think you need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not next to Mladic, I didn't watch TV either. I saw that statement of his among the material here at the trial and in my view, this statement doesn't make sense because there were no Dahijes there, there were no Turks there and as to what remains of the past he had in his mind, I don't know. Maybe he was involved in some sort of a third Serb uprising after Karadjordje [Realtime transcript read in error "Karadzic"] and Milos, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it in your times with him that you described Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vijo Gora, did he give you any indication of what he had in mind for the Muslim population, including the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't recount his statements to me. You could see in the footage how my first encounter with him commenced and how it ended. Something similar happened in the meeting in Bratunac on the 11th, in Vijo Gora, it was the same, a monologue delivered by Mladic, therefore he didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt but there may be a rather important transcription error at line 22. I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. He mentioned one of the kings, Karadjordjevic or something like that he mentioned. You have Karadzic there on line 22, and it was certainly not Karadzic; it was Karadjordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karadjordje, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. It's a simple correction that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now you have testified that on the evening of 11 July you drove through Potocari through a crowd of Muslims, went through Yellow Bridge and on to Bratunac and you came back the same way later that night; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go back but I didn't take the same route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why didn't you take the same route back?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had known what the situation would be on my way in, I wouldn't take it. Since I saw the situation and how dangerous it was, I didn't dare to take the same route but I rather chose a safer one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as I think you know but it's the position of the Prosecution that you did, in fact, make that trip but that you did it on the 12th of July and we'll get into a bit later. But when you went through that area which you say was the 11th of July, did you see any forces assembling around the area of Yellow Bridge preparing to go in the next morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing any forces. I know that there were men, soldiers, on the Serbian side at the checkpoint near the Yellow Bridge. I didn't know that any of our forces were being prepared to be brought in from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you went through Potocari, did you see any German Shepherd dogs amongst any of the troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you didn't see Mr. Borovcanin or his units at all around Yellow Brigade or Bratunac despite the evidence we've heard that they were coming into the area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when Mr. Borovcanin was with you on the 15th at the Standard and you sent him off to Baljkovica, were you aware, did he have dog units with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've seen the film of Potocari shot on the 12th which is the date that we believe you were in Potocari on the evening. You've seen large numbers or you've seen a number of German Shepherd dogs on that video; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey, I passed through Potocari on the 11th. I wasn't there on the 12th, therefore I couldn't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you've seen the video of the 12th where there were dogs in Potocari amongst the crowd being held by troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to be very careful when I speak about what I saw in reality and when I speak about the events from that period and finally what I've seen in the course of this trial. That is why I want to highlight this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand and I will try to make sure my questions highlight that distinction as well. So to be clear, what I'm talking about is your viewing the video, did you see the dogs in the video that was shot of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this footage here and I think that there are dogs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And of course it's the position of the Prosecutor that you went through on the 12th, but in that regard, can you tell us who do you think those dogs belonged to? What units?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the footage that I've seen and the trial so far, I can tell you that they belonged to a MUP unit. At the time, I didn't know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 4104.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this is a one-page document, General. I will have bigger documents for you and I -- this is something that I'm just responding to now. So if you could help us with this, we see that it is from the Ministry of the Interior, dated 12 July, to the commander for centre for breeding and training of police dogs. It's entitled: "In order to take over tasks of the mopping up the terrain in the Srebrenica section." It says: "Urgently dispatch all available guides and police dogs to the Srebrenica sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go up in English a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Upon arrival in Srebrenica, contact Ljubisa Borovcanin, deputy commander of the CBP who commands the police forces in Srebrenica and make arrangements on what to do next. "In accordance with the previous dispatch, you need to leave two guides with police dogs at the centre for tasks in the area of Sokolac. "Guides with police dogs need to report to Srebrenica by 0600. "Send a dispatch to the police forces staff headquarters in Pale quoting the above reference to notify them once the engaged troops and police dogs have been dispatched to the terrain." By Tomislav Kovac. So does this correspond to your opinion that these were MUP dogs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this dispatch is self-explanatory, it says that dogs should be dispatched. I didn't know at all if they had this centre for breeding and training dogs, where it was. I don't know when this was written. It says by 6.00 on the 12th, whether it's 6.00 in the morning or 6.00 in the afternoon, I don't know, but it's obviously -- the document obviously speaks about police dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this does correspond to your opinion that they -- these dogs on the 12th in Potocari were MUP dogs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that the footage that I see, I cannot say that it refers to the 12th or not. We saw dogs in this film, dogs are mentioned in this document, and this document was produced by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know that -- whether or not dogs, MUP dogs were used in the clearing of the -- or sweeping of the terrain from 17, 18, 19 July in the Zvornik area with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not in Baljkovica. I didn't see a single dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have a good professional relationship with General Krstic during this time period?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a standard official relationship, nothing special about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I ask you that because we saw in 65 ter 1206 A is the English, 1206 C is the B/C/S, that's the 17 July intercept where you have a short discussion with General Krstic and we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can get that up on the screen. It's the bottom part in the English that I want to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's very simple, General -- page 2 in the B/C/S. I'm -- I hope you can see this but I'm just referring to the part when Krstic gets on the radio and says, "This is Krstic." And you say, "Hello, General, sir." He says, "Hello, Vinko, Vinko." So he's referring to you by your first name which is more than just an official relationship; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree, Mr. McCloskey, and allow me to explain this kind of relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about what we call military mannerisms by officers, the superior officers normally addressed the low-ranking officers by their first name. Mr. Mladic even called me "little boy." That was just a customary way of addressing, that's why he addressed me as Vinko. Even when we were together as brigade commanders we were not friends, we did not socialise. He was much older than I was and he believed that, in a way, he may treat me as a junior officer not only in terms of my rank but also in terms of my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he also says going down further, "It's going fine but it would be better if you were there too." This isn't an official kind of a comment. He's saying it would be better if you were there with him. Then he goes on and says, "Take care of that and we'll see what -- bud," which is another informal way of dealing with someone, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he says "you" he is not addressing me personally, he is talking in plural which means referring to my unit. Krstic often used the word "burazer," or "brother," one form of the word "brother." He also used the word "chief." I didn't like these terms and I didn't want to call anyone chief, particularly in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as you've said, you met with his defence team. Did you meet with him in those days that you were meeting with his defence team?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was here at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you speak to him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was impossible for me to call him and he didn't call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't think if you had asked the defence team to get him on the phone, they would have been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't ask for him to call me so that I can speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 330, and that is the 16 July interim combat report and I would like page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, as that's coming up, I hope we don't -- I know we've seen over the years that especially officers, I think, both the VRS and BiH don't like repeating themselves and being asked to repeat themselves. That obviously gets annoying and I hope we don't have to do too much of that but I'm sure you understand that we will be going over some of the same ground and I may ask you, I probably already have, to repeat yourself somewhat, but it is normally because I have, perhaps, a different slant or take on it that I want to bring out. Okay. And what -- you've talked a lot about this interim report, and I don't need to hear all of it again, but what I do want to particularly point out, I believe it's in paragraph 3, and it's where you state when you're talking about the opening of the corridor: "It is likely that a certain number of soldiers got out among the civilians, but all who passed, passed through unarmed." I think you have said that that statement was false, that that was not true.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that as we have seen when the corridor was opened up, everyone that could got out and that would have included soldiers and those that may have had guns took them with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen them myself passing by and bearing arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you boldly wrote down in this report to General Krstic something you knew to be a lie.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once the passion simmered down I expect people react in a different way. I formulated this as I did at the time because I thought that was a better solution at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But to answer my question, you boldly told him a rather significant lie in this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the decision was mine and I took it on my own, and I knew that he definitely wouldn't agree with it at first -- at least initially, I had no other option but to send him a false report as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my question is this: You've told us that on the 15th of July, you were -- really after you got up there and got a look at what was going on, that you were -- had decided to open a corridor but you didn't do it until the next morning or the next morning, early afternoon on the 16th; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You did not seek authorisation from General Krstic before opening the corridor, did you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why, when you opened the corridor on the 16th, why didn't you seek authorisation from General Krstic? You had had many men killed by that point. Why did you not call him up and seek his authorisation to open up a corridor? Why instead did you choose to lie to him? First part -- I'm sorry that's a two-part question. Let me hit you with the first one. Why did you not call him and seek his authorisation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he had given me a clear task. If I asked him what I would do, he said he would have told me, You know what to do. You have my order. And for that reason, I did this on my own initiative. I already had that idea on the 15th but I was just waiting for a good opportunity and a good reason that people around me would be aware of so that in the future, someone would be able to say yes, Vinko acted properly although it was in contravention of the order that he had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I understand that on the night of the 15th, you had clear orders and nothing significant had changed. But by the morning of the 16th, the battle had occurred. I don't want to get into the details of that battle with you. You will agree with me that Serb soldiers died. Why didn't you at that time call General Krstic and seek authorisations? Why would you choose to lie?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, by the moment when I resumed my talks with Semso, I had no idea how many men had been killed; however, the decisive information to reestablish contact with Semso was the one given to me by Obrenovic which he had received from Semso Salihovic, an officer from the 28th Division, which spoke about a disastrous situation in the 28th Division. I didn't seek authorisation from anyone. I took this decision independently and I acted on my own. Simply, it was my personal choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand but why did you not seek authorisation after the battle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't seek authorisation because I believed that I wouldn't be granted one. I would just be told, You are not carrying out your tasks. Either you are afraid or what's happening to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you felt you knew General Krstic wanted that column fought and destroyed and that he would say no to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task that he had issued me. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know that if that's the task General Krstic had in mind, fighting and destroying that column, we can reasonably conclude that that was the Main Staff's order as well, can't we?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably Krstic received such an order from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you described "destroy" for us in the military context, and correct me if I am wrong, but in this context it would have meant killing the enemy and taking them prisoner.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean to bring them into such a state that they no longer pose a military threat. This can be achieved either by physical destruction in combat, certain percentage, but it can also be achieved by taking prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so as you sit here today, what do you believe would have happened to any prisoners that you would have taken pursuant to your orders to destroy the column on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an order first to capture and then destroy. If all these men had been captured, I wouldn't have a solution for them. I wouldn't know where to put them because there were no such facilities in the area of Zvornik capable of accommodating such a large number of people. I would ask the corps command either to arrange for an immediate exchange or to let those people free. I decided to let them pass through without capturing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If General Krstic and General Mladic had issued orders to have all the prisoners in Zvornik killed from the 14th to the 16th, would it be really possible for you to request of General Krstic to allow military-aged men to walk scot-free through a corridor?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a conditional question, "if", I must tell you that this situation did not occur. And we are not talking about prisoners. Some members of the 28th Division could have become prisoners on the 16th but it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You see, Colonel, it's the Prosecution's position that you're not a man that issues lies to his superiors lightly and that the reason you did it is because you knew that there was no way they were going to go along with it. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, Mr. McCloskey, I never lied to my superior officers. That would create serious consequences for the VRS army. I wrote this report as it is in order to assuage the concerns that my superiors had. During the war and my experience, I know that things are easily forgotten after the fact and that nothing would happen with the passage of time. That is why I wrote this report in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't seek authorisation from them because you know there was no way they were going to give it; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they would have given it or not I can only speculate. At that time, I thought that it was best for me not to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're now saying it's possible they would have said, All right, General, we don't want you to lose any more of your troops, let's let these guys through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, you see this is a situation that we can only speculate about. We will never learn the truth because this was already water under the bridge. At that time, I decided contrary to the claims by certain Defence counsel here who purport that I will walk over dead bodies in order to reach a goal. I could have shed blood in Baljkovica in order to carry out my orders, but that's not the kind of man I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a simple question, General. I'll try it again. Do you think there's any way that Krstic was going to allow you to open a corridor? You've been very clear on that except for your answer that you just made so I want you to think about this carefully.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a simple question, it still doesn't mean that the answer to it is going to be simple. It's usually just the contrary. I can only assume, based on my experience and my knowledge that I gained during the war, and I can assume on the order given to me that Krstic would have not agreed to me opening the corridor. I have my sincere doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Another option you had before you was to tell the truth. You could have, in that report, said what you said and you could have been truthful; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the truth was communicated to him subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But again, General, why didn't you choose the truth? You had it there. You were in command. Your men were dying. Why didn't you tell him the truth? Why did you choose to lie?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent the report in the form I did in order to repel any danger from myself as a person who refused to carry out an order. That was my decision at that moment, and it could have been different, of course, but it was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't tell the truth because you chose instead to repel any danger from yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that moment when things were happening the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What possible danger was it to you to put the truth in your interim combat report of 16 July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, without any previous explanation whatsoever, it would have been clear to everybody that I failed to carry out my orders. Second of all, the situation could have become more complicated, so much so that my initiative could have resulted in such terrible consequences on the Zvornik Brigade and even wider that I would have been in real danger as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you told General Krstic the truth, would you have been in danger from General Krstic or his superior command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first be held accountable by my superior, General Krstic. I don't know; whether there would be any pressure put on him by his superiors, I don't know; however, if we go back to that conversation that we just saw, or the conversation on the 16th in the morning in which he said, They are all armed, boss, keep pounding away at them. So, he told me already back then, keep pounding away at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is again simple and I think we can face it right now. Had you told him the truth that you were -- decided because of your personal involvement to open a corridor and allow the enemy through, you very likely could have been relieved of duty then and there; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, your question is a bit different to your previous question. I said explicitly that I was to be held accountable first by Krstic and then his superior. And as for me being relieved of my duties because of that, if they had wanted to do that, they would have relieved me subsequently. Although I did hear information that some people were thinking along those lines, that that was an option on the table at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll go back to it. What danger was General Krstic to you? You are the one that's brought up repelling danger. What danger was Krstic to you? Don't like my answer that you would have been relieved, what was it? What was the danger you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A failure to carry out on order or a refusal to carry out an order especially during the time of war under such conditions imposes certain punishment. He could have punished me. And I didn't send my report in fear of being relieved, because nobody is very happy to command a brigade in the times of war. It's one of the most difficult positions to be in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. So you're now saying that the reason you did not tell him the truth and that the fear that you had was fear of punishment; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had been afraid -- this was not a classical fear, no, but as a professional soldier, I was not used to refusing to carry out an order. However, I had to find a logical explanation why I had failed to carry out an order. That was what I wanted to do. That's what I eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I agree with you, General, you had to find a logical way out of this, so you chose to lie. Why didn't you choose just to not say anything? You could have written in your 16 July report nothing about it. "We are still undergoing difficult situation with the enemy." I think I've seen that written about a thousand times, and just leave it. That was another choice you didn't make. Why didn't you just say nothing? Why did you have to lie?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we now are in asked and answered territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a brand new area of why he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, you can say why did you lie? Why didn't you tell the truth? Why didn't you say anything, which would in itself be a lie but you just ask him the same question over and over again and it's oppressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am not asking the same question. He had that choice. I think we can see that clearly and logically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fine with the question. It's a different question even though it seeks the kind of the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, it's the same lousy subject and I understand it is, but it's a different question. Why didn't you choose that way out, not say anything?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is impossible to send a report without saying something. Second of all, if I had been a lawyer, I -- I may have acted in that way; but I was a commander, a military commander, and my reasoning as a commander in the field and my reasoning as I sit here today in this courtroom are two completely different things. I really appreciate the way you work, the way I see you work and I would very much love to have a Peter on my Defence team in addition to all the good people that I already have, but I have to tell you how I see things from my perspective as I sit here, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I understand that you were acting as a General, you were taking control of the situation. It's the Prosecution's position you got through this by doing something that was counter to everything you have been raised on in the army, you lied to your superiors because you knew your superiors had death in mind and you had no way out. You had to lie to them so you could get your men safe because you knew Krstic, Mladic were killing people and there was no way they were going to say yes to you. Isn't that right, General? Can't we just deal with it? Give yourself the credit that is due, that we see in your 15 July report and your 18 July report. Stop the lying.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I'm not lying. What I'm telling you now is not a lie. Please find a single piece of evidence to prove that I'm lying. These are completely two different things. My report on the 16th and my testimony here is not the same lie. I am not lying now when I am talking to you. Give me some evidence to prove that I am lying. I told you that I have my reservations about the possibility of Krstic approving the opening of the corridor. I'm sure that Mladic would not have allowed me to do that. And if that was the only lie during the war, we should have only been so lucky. Reports are usually fabricated at all levels, they are all lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we'll get into the evidence and we'll get into Dragan Obrenovic, I give you Dragan Obrenovic and his guilty plea but I think it's probably a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll break now. The sitting will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
